opportunities.description_excerpt:
## Bounty: Fix CPU mining 64-thread cap on Windows (64+ logical cores)

**Tier:** M — 60,000 XTM

### Description

CPU mining tops out at 64 threads on Windows machines that have more than 64 logical cores. A user with 128 threads reported that only 64 were ever used, no matter what thread count they selected. The goal of this bounty is simple to state and hard to prove: **make Tari Universe actually use more than 64 threads on a Windows machine that has more than 64 logical cores.**

Windows splits machines with more than 64 logical processors into "processor groups" of at most 64 each, and a process that isn't group-aware only gets scheduled onto one group. On top of that, Rust's `std::thread::available_parallelism()` (which we use to count cores) undercounts past 64 on Windows for the same reason. The correct fix must count cores across all processor groups **and** ensure the miner threads actually run across them — however that is best achieved.

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] On a Windows machine with **more than 64 logical cores**, CPU mining uses **more than 64 threads** — up to the count the user selects, bounded by the machine's real logical core count
- [ ] Core count is determined accurately across all processor groups (not capped at 64 the way `available_parallelism()` is)
- [ ] No regression on machines with ≤64 cores, and no regression on macOS or Linux
- [ ] **The PR includes proof of a working result on real hardware:**
  - [ ] A screenshot proving the test machine's spec (Task Manager → Performance, or CPU-Z) showing **more than 64 logical cores**
  - [ ] Screenshots and/or xmrig log excerpts showing **more than 64 threads in active use** after the fix, on that machine

### Development Requirements

This bounty **cannot be developed or verified blind.**

declares its own tuple and a root meta test holds the two vocabularies equal — one vocabulary,

opportunities.title: Support collateral of any decimals with 256-bit mul_div intermediates in market-core
opportunities.description_excerpt:
## Overview

market-core assumes in several places that its collateral has 7 decimals, like Stellar Classic USDC. `MIN_SEED` is `100 * 10_000_000` (100 USDC at 7 decimals). `MAX_SETS` is `1e15` (100M USDC at 7 decimals). The overflow argument at the top of `math.rs` says every product of two quantities stays below 1e30, safely inside `i128`. None of that holds if the deployer passes a SEP-41 token with a different `decimals()`. Soroban-native tokens commonly use 18 decimals, and bridged assets vary.

With 18 decimals, `MIN_SEED` would be about 1e-9 tokens, so the spam-prevention floor disappears. `MAX_SETS` would cap a market at 0.001 tokens, so realistic markets could not be created. And if `MAX_SETS` were simply raised, `mul_div_floor(a, b, c)` would overflow `i128` on the `a * b` product long before the result itself overflows. Nothing warns the deployer: `__constructor` validates only `default_fee_bps`.

This issue makes market-core decimals-aware and makes its fixed-point helpers robust. Decimals are read once at deploy, the economic bounds are derived from them, and the multiply-divide helpers move to 256-bit intermediates so correctness no longer depends on the 1e30 headroom argument. The Python and TypeScript mirrors must stay in lockstep, because agents and frontends quote off-chain.

## Background & current behavior

Paths are relative to `oracledesk-stellar/`.

- `contracts/market-core/src/lib.rs`:
  - `const MIN_SEED: i128 = 100 * 10_000_000;`, documented as "100 USDC (7 decimals)".
  - `__constructor(admin, collateral, treasury, resolver, default_fee_bps)` stores `DataKey::Collateral` and never calls into the token.
  - `create_market` checks `(MIN_SEED..=MAX_SETS).contains(&seed_amount)`. `buy` checks `new_sets > MAX_SETS` → `Error::MarketTooLarge` (#15).

opportunities.description_excerpt:
## Overview

Creating a market in OracleDesk costs the creator nothing beyond the seed liquidity. `create_market` requires `seed_amount ≥ MIN_SEED` (100 USDC at 7 decimals), but the creator is also the sole LP, and the seed comes back through `claim_pool_remainder` once the market is final. That includes the case where the market is **voided**. A creator can therefore commit to an unrevealable `resolution_hash`, an ambiguous question, or a resolution spec pointing at an oracle they control, attract trading, and bear no penalty when the guardian steps in with `resolver::guardian_void_market`. The only deterrent today is the guardian's attention.

A creation bond is the standard remedy. The creator posts an additional amount at creation, held separately from the market's trading collateral. The bond is refunded when the market resolves normally, or is voided through a non-fault path, and forfeited to the fee recipient when the guardian voids the market for cause. That aligns creators' incentives with producing resolvable markets, and gives the guardian an economic lever rather than only a binary one.

The engineering problem crosses all three money-moving contracts. Market-core has to learn *why* a market was voided (today `void_market(market_id)` carries no reason). The resolver has to pass that reason across the vendored-wasm boundary (ADR 0002). Treasury has to fund bonds for `agent_create_market` within its risk caps. Bond accounting also has to stay strictly separate from the per-market solvency invariant (`balance == sets_minted + fees_accrued`).

opportunities.title: Add per-market circuit breakers: max price impact per trade and per-ledger price bands
opportunities.description_excerpt:
## Overview

market-core's FPMM pools are thin by design. The minimum seed is `MIN_SEED = 100 USDC`, and the agent-created markets on testnet are seeded with small amounts. In such a pool a single `buy` can move the YES price from 50% to 99% in one call, and nothing in the contract objects. That is a legitimate trade from the AMM's point of view, but for OracleDesk it is a real attack surface:

- **LP griefing.** An attacker can push the price to an extreme right before `close_time`, leaving the LP (often the treasury) holding the losing side, then unwind after any off-chain reaction.
- **Price-reading consumers.** `get_price` is spot. Any frontend, agent (`MarketState.yesBps`) or downstream contract that reads it can be shown a manipulated number within a single transaction.
- **Fat-finger agent trades.** `agents/bin/trader.ts` currently submits `min_shares_out: 0n`, so a bug in sizing could move a market arbitrarily.

This issue adds two circuit breakers, both snapshotted per market so they cannot be changed after trading begins. The first is a **max price impact per trade**: one call cannot move the price more than `max_impact_bps`. The second is a **per-ledger price band**: once cumulative movement within one ledger exceeds `band_bps` from the price at the start of that ledger, further trades in that ledger revert. Both must be cheap, deterministic in both trade directions, and impossible to turn into a permanent lock by an attacker.

## Background & current behavior

Paths are relative to `oracledesk-stellar/`.

- `contracts/market-core/src/lib.rs`:
  - `buy` and `sell` run `assert_not_paused`, `require_auth`, `load_market`, `assert_tradable`, then `math::calc_buy` / `calc_sell`, then effects and the transfer. The only bounds are `min_shares_out` / `max_shares_in`

opportunities.description_excerpt:
## Overview

OracleDesk now has two incompatible payment flows. Per-trace unlocks use x402, the HTTP-402 standard for paid resources: the client hits the resource, receives `PaymentRequirements`, pays, and retries with an `X-PAYMENT` header, and a facilitator verifies and settles. The contracts repo's `x402/trace-api.ts` implements it with `@x402/express` `paymentMiddleware` and the `exact` Stellar scheme. The daily pass instead uses a bespoke flow. The frontend builds a raw USDC `transfer` to `PAYMENTS_RECIPIENT`, has the wallet sign and submit it, then posts the hash to `POST /traces/:id/unlock`, and the backend reverse-engineers the transaction in `verifyUsdcTransfer()`.

The bespoke flow has known weaknesses:

- the user pays first and only learns afterward whether the backend accepts the payment (allowance refusals, a wrong recipient, or a stale price all become paid-but-refused);
- the backend has to parse envelopes defensively;
- there's a two-step window where funds move and no claim follows;
- integrators (agents, scripts) can't use standard x402 clients to buy a pass.

Verification happens *before* settlement, so a refused purchase never moves funds. ## Overview

Every trace preview from `GET /traces/:id` includes `unlockPriceRaw`, which the frontend shows as the per-trace price. That value comes from `PER_TRACE_PRICE_RAW = 50_000n` (0.005 USDC), a constant hard-coded in `src/services/subscription.service.ts`. The per-trace sale itself happens in the contracts repo's x402 service, which charges `TRACE_PRICE_USDC` from its own env (default `"0.01"` in `x402/server.ts`, i.e. `100000` base units). So today the UI shows 0.005 USDC and the wallet asks for 0.01 USDC. Users get one price in the UI and a different one at signing time, which looks like a bait-and-switch and erodes trust in a product whose selling point is verifiability.

The source of truth for what x402 charges is the x402 service itself. An unpaid request to a paid resource returns `402 Payment Required` with a `PaymentRequirements` body listing `scheme`, `network`, `asset`, `maxAmountRequired`, `payTo`, `resource`, and so on. - it fetches the requirements with a `HEAD` or `GET` and no payment;

The treasury contract holds the capital the autonomous agent trades with. opportunities.title: Add market-maker inventory management for creator seed shares and LP exposure
opportunities.description_excerpt:
## Overview

When the OracleDesk treasury creates a market through `agent_create_market`, it becomes the market's `creator`, which makes it both the sole liquidity provider and, whenever `initial_yes_bps != 5000`, the holder of a directional position. `math::seed_reserves` mints `seed_amount` complete sets, keeps fewer of the *likelier* outcome in the pool, and gives the leftover to the creator. A market seeded at 75% YES with 150 USDC puts about 100 USDC of YES shares into the treasury's `Position`, plus a pool whose final value depends on which side wins.

The market-maker never looks at either of these. After creating a market it forgets about it, so the treasury's real exposure (creator position plus LP pool remainder) is unmanaged. If the crowd pushes YES down from 75% to 40%, the treasury holds a large YES position bought at an implied 75%, and its pool now holds even more YES. A real market maker would rebalance by selling inventory when the price moves through its fair value, within risk limits.

This issue adds an inventory module that computes the treasury's combined, scenario-dependent exposure per market, and a policy that sells down directional inventory through `agent_sell`. It also adds the missing `agentSell` adapter path. The hard part is that LP value has no closed form under trading. The pool remainder at settlement is `settle_value(outcome, reserve_yes, reserve_no)`, so exposure must be evaluated per scenario (YES, NO, Void). Selling inventory into its own pool also moves the price *against the treasury's LP position*, so naive "sell until flat" can lose more on the pool than it saves on the position.

opportunities.description_excerpt:
## Context

The API can already export its request spans over OTLP/HTTP JSON. The exporter has no dependencies, is off by default and is switched on with `SPACE_OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` (`apps/api/src/otlp-span-exporter.ts`). When the API starts a Temporal workflow it passes a W3C `traceparent` in the workflow input and in the Temporal memo (`apps/api/src/turns.ts`, `workflowCorrelationMemo` in `apps/api/src/trace-context.ts`). The worker reads it for its structured activity logs (`apps/worker/src/activity-observability.ts`).

But the trace stops at the API. Workers emit no spans, so a slow or failing Room Agent mission, chat turn or memory repair can only be followed by joining log lines by hand. [`docs/quality/observability.md`](https://github.com/oll4com/spaceapp/blob/main/docs/quality/observability.md#not-covered) lists this under "Not covered": "Span export covers API requests only" and "Background continuations start a new trace". In [`KNOWN_LIMITATIONS.md`](https://github.com/oll4com/spaceapp/blob/main/docs/quality/KNOWN_LIMITATIONS.md) this is OBS-001 / OBS-007: "worker/host spans" are still open.

## Goal

With `SPACE_OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` set, one API request that starts work on Temporal produces **one connected trace**: the API SERVER span, then the workflow execution, then every activity attempt. The trace shows in any OTLP backend (Jaeger, Tempo, Honeycomb, ...) without extra glue.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every Temporal worker process in `apps/worker` (`worker.ts`, `memory-maintenance-worker.ts`, `memory-mutation-worker.ts`) exports spans to `<endpoint>/v1/traces` when `SPACE_OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` is set, and does nothing when it is not.
- [ ] The exporter has the same guarantees as the API exporter: a bounded queue that drops spans
